turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Declan, I did your checks before we came in. Blood pressure is 146 over 84, pulse 72, temperature 36.8. The pharmacy technician left the printed list with me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit down. This is only the repeat prescription review, nothing fancy.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah I'm grand, Doctor. Hardly worth coming, it's only a niggle in the knee. The bus was late again, but that's neither here nor there.
[SEG0004] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He'll say that. It's the right knee, and the stairs have him holding the banister every morning. I'm in weekdays.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): The right knee, so. When did it actually start?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Last winter, or the one before. I couldn't give you a date. Sure I don't keep track of these things.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): No date, then. And day to day, how bad is the pain?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): It's nothing. A small ache in the right knee on the stairs, and the tablets sort it. I'm not one to complain.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Small ache, he says. He takes the stairs one at a time. Still gets himself out to the shop, mind.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking for the knee at the minute?

[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Five hundred milligrams... no, two of the five hundreds, so a gram, four times a day. I was on the co-codamol 8/500 for a bit and I knocked that on the head.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Co-codamol stopped, paracetamol a gram four times a day. Anything else?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): The naproxen, 500 milligrams twice a day, with the food. And omeprazole 20 milligrams once in the morning, so the naproxen doesn't catch my stomach.
[SEG0014] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, the chemist list the technician printed has naproxen 250 milligrams twice daily. Paracetamol, omeprazole and the blood pressure one match what I'm hearing.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): They've it wrong, so. I take the 500. Or maybe the box is 250 and I take two, I don't be reading boxes. It's all the same, isn't it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's not all the same, and I won't guess. We'll park the naproxen dose. The blood pressure tablet, what is that one?
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Amlodipine, 5 milligrams, once a day. I set the box up in the mornings and he doesn't miss that one.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Five, yeah. The pressure is nothing. I live on my own, she comes weekdays, that's more than enough fuss.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other tablets, anything bought in the chemist?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Not a thing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to a medicine?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None at all.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): With the naproxen, any heartburn, any black stools?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Not a bit. Stomach's grand.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): And chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No, no. I'm well able for a walk. The waiting room was freezing, mind you, but I'm grand.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at the knee now. There's a small swelling over the right knee, no redness, it bends nearly the whole way, and the pulses in the foot are fine.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): There you are. Nothing in it.
[SEG0029] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He still asked me in the car about a stronger tablet. Tramadol, or the strong co-codamol, whichever you'd give.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): I only mentioned it. Well, actually, if you've something stronger I won't say no, but I'm not pushed. It's a niggle.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not prescribing tramadol, and I'm not moving you to co-codamol 30/500. You're seventy-one, you're already on naproxen, and you can still walk. A stronger painkiller isn't the right call.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Fair enough. I wasn't bothered either way.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): What I will renew today is the paracetamol, a gram four times a day, the omeprazole 20 milligrams each morning, and the amlodipine 5 milligrams once a day. I will not sign the naproxen until we know if it's 250 or 500.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): I can ring the chemist this afternoon and ask them which strength is on the actual prescription.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do that, please. Don't let the naproxen go out until they confirm it.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back so we're clear. The right knee pain, you can't date it, last winter or the winter before, mild in your own words. Paracetamol a gram four times daily, co-codamol 8/500 stopped, naproxen twice a day but 500 from you and 250 on the list, omeprazole 20 in the morning, amlodipine 5, no drug allergies, no heartburn, no black stools, no chest pain, no breathlessness. I'm calling it a flare of the osteoarthritis you already have, nothing separate, and no stronger tablet.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Osteoarthritis, yeah, that's years. The blood pressure is ongoing as well, sure it's no bother.

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks... no, the repeat review is three months, so three months. If the knee goes red and hot and swollen, or you pass black stools, ring the surgery the same day. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0039] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch him for that. I can bring the naproxen box in, if it helps ye.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): There'll be no need for drama. I'm grand. Three months is fine.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
